notes.meaning: The men of Ephraim crossed the Jordan River to confront Jephthah. They were jealous and angry that he had defeated Ammon without inviting them, and they threatened to burn down his house with him inside. Their pride drove them to pick a fight with a brother tribe instead of rejoicing over God's victory.

Jephthah answered that he had actually called for their help against Ammon, but they refused to come. Ephraim had stayed safely away while the crisis raged, but now showed up to complain after the danger was past. Jephthah made it clear that their charges against him were completely false.

Seeing that Ephraim would not help, Jephthah risked his own life and marched out to battle. He emphasized that the Lord gave the victory over the Ammonites, not human strength alone. Since God had clearly fought for Gilead, Ephraim was actually fighting against God's work by attacking him.

Jephthah gathered the Gileadite army and fought Ephraim. The Gileadites were deeply angered because the Ephraimites insulted them as runaways and outcasts. Unlike Gideon, who calmed Ephraim with gentle words, Jephthah answered pride with war, leading to a tragic civil conflict.

The Gileadites took control of the shallow crossing points along the Jordan River to cut off Ephraim's retreat. Whenever a runaway soldier tried to cross back home and denied being an Ephraimite, the guards tested him. The very people who had sneered at Gilead were now desperate fugitives themselves.

The Gileadites asked each suspect to say the word 'Shibboleth,' which means a flowing stream. Because people from Ephraim spoke with a different regional dialect, they could only pronounce it 'Sibboleth,' giving away their identity. The guards killed them immediately at the river crossings, and 42,000 Ephraimites fell during this war.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that the Hebrew word for thousand can also mean a military unit or squad, meaning forty-two units were lost rather than 42,000 individual soldiers.

notes.meaning: Jephthah led Israel as judge for six years before he died. He was given an honorable burial in his home region of Gilead. Even though his life included deep sorrow and bitter strife, Scripture remembers him as a deliverer who trusted the Lord.

After Jephthah's death, Ibzan of Bethlehem became the judge over Israel. His leadership began a long season of quiet and peace for the nation. Unlike the warrior judges, his rule was not defined by major wars or foreign oppression.

Ibzan had thirty sons and thirty daughters, and he arranged marriages for all of them outside his clan. These marriages brought in new family ties and built peaceful alliances with other groups. In contrast to Jephthah's lonely grief over his only daughter, Ibzan enjoyed a large, flourishing household.

Ibzan died after leading the people for seven years and was buried in his hometown of Bethlehem. His years as judge were quiet and steady. Living a peaceful and useful life in service to God is a quiet blessing for any community.

Elon from the northern tribe of Zebulun became the next judge of Israel. He led the nation for ten peaceful years. God often used quiet leaders from different tribes to keep order and preserve worship among His people.

Elon died at the end of his ten years as judge and was buried in Aijalon within his tribal homeland of Zebulun. This town was in the north, distinct from the better-known Aijalon in Dan. His peaceful burial marked the close of another steady chapter in Israel's story.

Abdon son of Hillel became judge after Elon. He was from the town of Pirathon in the territory of Ephraim. His appointment showed that God still raised up leaders from Ephraim despite their earlier defeat under Jephthah.

Abdon had forty sons and thirty grandsons who rode on seventy donkeys, and he judged Israel for eight years. In that culture, riding well-bred donkeys was a sign of high rank, honor, and wealth. His large and prosperous family helped him oversee the land and maintain justice throughout his peaceful rule.

Abdon died and was buried in his hometown of Pirathon in Ephraim, in an area once held by the Amalekites. His death brought to a close a long span of thirty-one years of rest under minor judges. God faithfully preserved the nation in peace during these quiet years before new trials arose.
